primaryText: A conductor is Dudamel
translation: A conductor is Dudamel
comment: Marked # by Cooper: truth-conditionally equivalent to Dudamel is a conductor by the compositional contents (94), but the construction-based content conductor(d) (92a) is available only to the latter.

primaryText: Mary should eat her broccoli
translation: Mary should eat her broccoli
comment: Portner's example: bouletic when the fact that Mary loves broccoli is at issue, deontic when children are to eat everything on their plates; the deontic and the bouletic topos (28) each witness the necessity (29).

primaryText: Every dog ran into the field. They had seen the rabbits.
discourseSegments: Every dog ran into the field.
translation: Every dog ran into the field. They had seen the rabbits.
comment: Plural discourse anaphora to a universal antecedent: a bare function witness for every yields no witness set for they to pick up.

primaryText: A dog is barking. It is right outside my window
discourseSegments: It is right outside my window
translation: A dog is barking. It is right outside my window
comment: Singular anaphora to the x-field of the particular witness (63).

primaryText: Some dogs are barking. They are right outside my window.
discourseSegments: They are right outside my window.
translation: Some dogs are barking. They are right outside my window.
comment: Plural anaphora to the witness set of the general condition (65); no particular condition is needed.

primaryText: No dog barked. They were all busy gnawing on a bone.
discourseSegments: They were all busy gnawing on a bone.
translation: No dog barked. They were all busy gnawing on a bone.
comment: They picks up the witness set of type every-w(dog'), the dogs which did not bark: complement set anaphora (Moxey and Sanford), evidence for the particular condition (70) over the general one (67).

primaryText: Every dog barked. They had been disturbed by the intruder.
discourseSegments: They had been disturbed by the intruder.
translation: Every dog barked. They had been disturbed by the intruder.
comment: Plural discourse anaphora predicted by the general condition (72).

primaryText: Most dogs bark when somebody unknown comes into their territory. They are disturbed by an intruder.
discourseSegments: Most dogs bark when somebody unknown comes into their territory.
They are disturbed by an intruder.
translation: Most dogs bark when somebody unknown comes into their territory. They are disturbed by an intruder.
comment: They refers to the witness set containing most dogs (REFSET) or to dogs in general (MAXSET); Cooper leaves the source of the MAXSET reading unresolved.

primaryText: Most dogs bark when somebody unknown comes into their territory. They never feel threatened whatever happens.
discourseSegments: Most dogs bark when somebody unknown comes into their territory.
They never feel threatened whatever happens.
translation: Most dogs bark when somebody unknown comes into their territory. They never feel threatened whatever happens.
comment: Cooper's # marks the COMPSET reading: they cannot refer to the dogs which do not bark (Nouwen), consistent with the general condition (74).

primaryText: Few dogs in the kennels barked. They didn't hear the intruder.
discourseSegments: Few dogs in the kennels barked.
translation: Few dogs in the kennels barked. They didn't hear the intruder.
comment: COMPSET anaphora predicted by the particular condition (85)–(86) with the complement witness set.

primaryText: Few congressmen admire Kennedy, and they are very junior.
translation: Few congressmen admire Kennedy, and they are very junior.
comment: Quoted by Cooper from Nouwen's discussion of Evans: REFSET anaphora with few, predicted by the general condition (79)–(80) rather than the particular one.

primaryText: A few dogs barked. They had heard the intruder.
translation: A few dogs barked. They had heard the intruder.
comment: REFSET anaphora predicted by the general condition (89)–(90).

primaryText: A few dogs barked. They hadn't heard the intruder
translation: A few dogs barked. They hadn't heard the intruder
comment: Cooper's # marks the COMPSET reading: they cannot refer to the dogs that did not bark, since only the general condition is available.

primaryText: A dog barked. They do when they notice an intruder.
discourseSegments: They do when they notice an intruder.
translation: A dog barked. They do when they notice an intruder.
comment: They is dogs in general, the restr path of the content (102); Cooper: we could potentially have all of the anaphora in (103).

primaryText: A dog barked. It heard an intruder.
translation: A dog barked. It heard an intruder.
comment: It is the dog which barked, the x-field of the witness (100).

primaryText: No dog barked. They normally do when they notice an intruder.
discourseSegments: They normally do when they notice an intruder.
translation: No dog barked. They normally do when they notice an intruder.
comment: They is dogs in general, the restr path of the content (107).

primaryText: No dog barked. They did not hear the intruder.
discourseSegments: They did not hear the intruder.
translation: No dog barked. They did not hear the intruder.
comment: They is the dogs which did not bark, the X-field of the witness (106).

primaryText: Few dogs barked. They normally do when they notice an intruder.
discourseSegments: They normally do when they notice an intruder.
translation: Few dogs barked. They normally do when they notice an intruder.
comment: They is dogs in general, the restr path of the content (112).

primaryText: Few dogs barked. They did not hear the intruder.
discourseSegments: They did not hear the intruder.
translation: Few dogs barked. They did not hear the intruder.
comment: They is the dogs which did not bark, the X-field of the witness (111); Cooper notes, after an anonymous referee, a possible garden-path effect on this reading.

primaryText: every boy hugged a dog
translation: every boy hugged a dog
comment: (1a) every boy is such that there is a dog he hugged, (1b) there is a dog every boy hugged: the content type has both as witnesses.

primaryText: a boy hugged every dog
translation: a boy hugged every dog
comment: (2b) is the reading with the boy outermost; the wide scope of every dog comes from storage (17) and retrieval (19).

primaryText: No dog which chases a cat catches it
translation: No dog which chases a cat catches it
comment: Donkey anaphora treated as discourse anaphora within the scope property (54)–(55): no dog catches any cat it chases.

primaryText: No dog which chases every cat catches it
translation: No dog which chases every cat catches it
comment: Cooper: it is difficult to relate the singular pronoun to every cat, as in the discourse anaphora of (46d).

primaryText: No dog which chases every cat catches them
translation: No dog which chases every cat catches them
comment: The plural pronoun relates to every cat, as in the discourse anaphora of (46e).

primaryText: Every cat miaowed. It wanted milk.
translation: Every cat miaowed. It wanted milk.
comment: Cooper: it is difficult to relate the singular pronoun to every cat.

primaryText: Every cat miaowed. They wanted milk.
translation: Every cat miaowed. They wanted milk.
comment: The plural pronoun relates easily to every cat.

primaryText: Every person who had a dime put it in the parking meter
translation: Every person who had a dime put it in the parking meter
comment: Does not suggest that anyone who had several dimes put them all in the meter: the weak reading, from the existential purification (59).

primaryText: Every man who has a daughter thinks she is the most beautiful girl in the world
translation: Every man who has a daughter thinks she is the most beautiful girl in the world
comment: Does not commit a man with two daughters to the contradictory belief that each is the one most beautiful girl.

primaryText: Every man who owned a slave owned his offspring
translation: Every man who owned a slave owned his offspring
comment: A modification of an example in Heim (1990), which Chierchia uses to argue for the strong reading, from the universal purification (60), (66): one man owning a slave but not the slave's offspring falsifies it. Cooper finds the case of a slave with several offspring, one owned by somebody else, unclear.

primaryText: Sam likes him
translation: Sam likes him
comment: Principle B: him cannot be anaphorically related to Sam within the clause, though the two may refer to the same individual, as when Sam likes the person described on a page he does not realise is about himself.

primaryText: A man walked. He whistled.
translation: A man walked. He whistled.
comment: Cross-sentential anaphora: the previous content is merged into the context under the label for the previous utterance and the pronoun's path identified with the man's.

primaryText: No girl thinks she failed
translation: No girl thinks she failed
comment: The stored no girl leaves a pronoun path in the context which anaphoric combination relates to she; retrieval quantifies over the property of being a girl who thinks she failed.
